content: Tables should be employed to present precise values of data that cannot be effectively summarized in a few sentences or when the goal is to demonstrate specific interrelationships. However, tables should not be used if the data can be easily incorporated into the text, as tables are more costly to typeset than text. Additionally, tables are unnecessary when the data lacks relationships or time sequences. A table should be comprehensible without requiring reference to the main text. After reading the title and abstract, many readers often review tables and illustrations to decide whether to read the full text. Each table should be cited in the text, numbered sequentially, and accompanied by a title that accurately describes its content. Column and row headings should be concise or abbreviated, and footnotes should be included to explain non-standard abbreviations or to identify statistical measures of variation, such as standard deviation or standard error of the mean. Tables should follow a logical structure, such as reflecting the sequence of data collection or changes over time, and should avoid unnecessary words or repetition of headings in their titles. Ambiguity regarding the purpose of the columns and rows should be avoided. When column headings are grouped, a straddle-line should be used to clarify which headings fall under the grouped column headings. Row headings may be indented to indicate groupings. For publication purposes, tables should not exceed the width of the journal columns. A single-column table in a double-column journal should not contain more than 60 characters (including spaces) per row, while a full-page-width table should not exceed 120 characters per row. Each table should be typed or printed with double-spacing on a separate sheet of paper and should not be submitted as photographs or images. Internal horizontal and vertical rules should be avoided. Tables should be numbered consecutively in the order of their first citation in the text, and each table must be cited in the text. If data from another source is used, permission must be obtained and fully acknowledged. Excessive use of tables relative to the text length can complicate page layout. Authors should consult the journal to estimate the appropriate number of tables per 1,000 words of text, with a general guideline of no more than one table or illustration per 1,000 words (approximately four manuscript pages). Editors may recommend depositing additional tables with backup data in an archival service or making them available upon request, with an appropriate statement added to the text. Illustrations should serve a specific purpose, such as providing evidence to support an argument or presenting data more efficiently (e.g., flowcharts). Illustrations used solely for emphasis are not recommended and may be more suitable for presentations than written papers. Graphs are ideal for illustrating relationships, while tables are preferable for presenting exact values. When trends and relationships are more important than exact values, graphs are more efficient. A graph is a better alternative to a table with numerous entries. Data should not be duplicated in both figures and tables. For publication, figures should be professionally drawn and photographed; freehand or typewritten lettering is unacceptable. Authors should submit sharp, glossy, black-and-white photographic prints instead of original drawings, X-ray films, or other materials. Letters, numbers, and symbols should be clear, uniform, and of sufficient size to remain legible after reduction for publication. Titles and detailed explanations should be included in the legends, not on the illustrations themselves. Each figure should have a label on its back indicating the figure number, author’s name, and the top of the figure. Writing on the back of figures or damaging them with paper clips should be avoided. Figures should not be bent or mounted on cardboard. Photomicrographs should include internal scale markers, and symbols, arrows, or letters used in microphotographs should contrast with the background. If photographs of individuals are used, subjects must either be unidentifiable or provide written permission for their use. Figures should be numbered consecutively in the order of their first citation in the text. If a figure has been previously published, the original source must be acknowledged, and written permission from the copyright holder must be submitted. Permission is required regardless of authorship or publisher, except for public domain documents. For color illustrations, authors should verify the journal’s requirements for color negatives, transparencies, or prints. Some journals publish color illustrations only if the author covers the additional cost. Legends for illustrations should be typed or printed with double-spacing on a separate page, using Arabic numerals corresponding to the illustrations. Symbols, arrows, numbers, or letters used to identify parts of illustrations should be clearly explained in the legend. The internal scale and staining method in microphotographs should also be stated. The discussion and conclusions section of a paper should highlight the novel and significant aspects of the study and the conclusions derived from them. It should not repeat data or material already presented in the introduction or results sections. A well-structured discussion should include the following components: a statement of principal findings, strengths and weaknesses of the study, strengths and weaknesses in relation to other studies, the meaning of the study (including possible mechanisms and implications for clinicians and policymakers), unanswered questions and future research, and a conclusion. The discussion should begin with a clear statement of the principal findings, ideally in a few sentences, emphasizing the new information provided by the study. Strengths and weaknesses of the study should be addressed equally, as reviewers value authors’ acknowledgment of limitations. If weaknesses are not mentioned, readers may lose trust in the paper. Findings not described in the results section should not be discussed. Authors should critically evaluate their methodology, findings, and conclusions, particularly when differences in results compared to other studies are observed. Possible explanations for these differences should be offered, and if unknown, this should be stated without implying superiority of the results. The meaning of the study, possible mechanisms, and implications for clinicians and policymakers should be carefully written, avoiding overinterpretation of the evidence. Authors should emphasize what the results mean and what they do not mean to prevent unjustified conclusions. Unanswered questions and future research directions should be proposed, generating new ideas for further investigation. A simple statement that further research is needed is less helpful than providing specific research questions or suggesting particular studies. A strong conclusion should link back to the study’s goals and remain within its boundaries. Authors should avoid unqualified statements and unsupported conclusions, such as claims about economic benefits without including relevant data and analysis. Negative findings can be as important as positive ones. Acknowledgments should specify contributions that do not justify authorship, such as general support, technical help, or financial/material support, and disclose relationships that may pose conflicts of interest. Individuals who contributed intellectually but do not qualify for authorship may be named with their permission, describing their role (e.g., scientific adviser, critical review, data collection, or clinical trial participation). Authors are responsible for obtaining written permission from acknowledged individuals, as readers may infer their endorsement of the data and conclusions. The reference section is a critical part of a scientific paper. References should be limited to those directly relevant to the work described, with a maximum of 40 references for the longest papers. References should be carefully checked and verified against original documents, as errors can mislead readers. Authors are advised to photocopy the first page of each cited reference to ensure accurate citation. Different scientific disciplines use various citation formats, such as MLA, APA, CMS, and CBE styles. In biomedical sciences, the Harvard and Vancouver systems are commonly used. The Harvard system lists references alphabetically at the end of the paper, citing them in the text with the author’s name and publication year in parentheses. The Vancouver system numbers references consecutively in the order they are first mentioned in the text, using Arabic numerals in parentheses. Authors should use the Harvard style in early drafts and switch to the Vancouver style in the final draft to avoid renumbering references during revisions.
